title: Idioms and proverbs — saying more with less
title_target: Tak ada rotan, akar pun jadi
goal: Understand and use the idioms Indonesians reach for every day — *buah tangan, besar kepala, kambing hitam, lempar batu sembunyi tangan* — and a handful of proverbs (*peribahasa*) that still turn up in conversation, speeches and headlines.
bekal: recognise body-part idioms like *besar kepala*, *panjang tangan* and *buah tangan* and say what they really mean
use a proverb at the right moment: *Tak ada rotan, akar pun jadi*, *bagai air di daun talas*, *nasi sudah menjadi bubur*
talk about blame without blaming: *kambing hitam*, *menyalahkan*, *mengaku salah*, *bertanggung jawab*

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Buah tangan dari Magelang
dialogs.intro: A Saturday in late June. Sarah has come back to her house in Yogyakarta for the weekend without telling anyone. She knocks on Bu Endang's gate next door with a bag from Magelang.

notes: **Buah tangan** — “fruit of the hand” — is the polite, slightly literary word for a gift you bring when visiting. *Oleh-oleh* is the everyday word, especially for souvenirs from a trip. Arriving empty-handed after a journey is noticed in Indonesia; a small bag of the local speciality is enough.

**Repot-repot** — the standard modest protest when you receive a gift: *Aduh, pakai repot-repot segala* (“oh, you went to all this trouble”). The correct reply is to wave it away: *Ah, cuma sedikit, Bu* (it's only a little something).

**Tak ada rotan, akar pun jadi** — “if there's no rattan, a root will do”. Rattan was the proper material for tying and binding; a root is the humble substitute. It means making do with what you have, and it is kind here: Bu Endang is telling Sarah the salak is perfectly fine.

**Salim** is the gesture children make to elders and guests: taking the older person's right hand and touching it to the forehead or nose. *Salim dulu!* is what every Indonesian parent says when a child forgets. Dimas, like most children, forgets exactly when he wants a present.

**Besar kepala** — “big head” — means conceited, exactly like English “big-headed”. Its neighbour *keras kepala* (“hard head”) means stubborn. *Sombong* (arrogant, showing off) is the plain word, and one of the worst things you can call someone in Indonesia.

**Masuk telinga kanan, keluar telinga kiri** — “in the right ear, out the left” — is the English idiom with an extra direction. *Buktinya…* (“the proof is…”) is how Indonesians win an argument, or think they do. *Satu-kosong* is the football score “one-nil”.

grammars.title: Idioms built on the body
body: Indonesian builds many idioms from a body part plus an adjective or noun. The literal image is usually a good clue, but not always — *panjang tangan* is not someone with long arms.
after: ⚠️ *Ringan tangan* is genuinely two-faced: *Dia ringan tangan* can praise someone as always ready to help, or warn that they hit people. Context, and usually the rest of the sentence, decides.
Other body idioms worth knowing: *mata duitan* (money-grubbing, “money-eyed”), *tinggi hati* (proud, “high liver”), *kecil hati* (discouraged), *muka tembok* (shameless, “wall-faced”).

grammars.title: How a peribahasa works
body: A *peribahasa* is a traditional saying, often from Malay oral tradition. Many follow a pattern: *bagai / seperti* + a picture, or a two-part rhythm that sounds like a line of verse. Learn them whole; the grammar is often old-fashioned.

head: Peribahasa
Literally
Meaning
rows: no rattan, a root will do
make do with what you have
like water on a taro leaf
the rice has turned to porridge
kill two birds with one stone
like a betel nut split in two
as alike as two peas in a pod
rippling water shows it isn't deep

after: *Tak* is the short, literary form of *tidak*, and it is standard in proverbs and headlines. *Pun* after *akar* means “even”: “even a root will do”.
Use proverbs lightly. One at the right moment, especially from a foreigner, delights people; three in one conversation sounds like a school textbook.

dialogs.title: Second dialogue — Siapa yang salah?
dialogs.intro: The next Tuesday, back in Sumberwangi. The thirty new signposts in three languages, agreed at the meeting in May, have just arrived from the printer. Mas Bayu has come over from the Yogya office to help put them up.

lines.speaker: Yoga:
lines.text: Mbak, gawat. Papannya udah datang, tapi bahasa Inggrisnya salah ketik.
lines.id: Sarah, we've got a problem. The signs have arrived, but there's a typo in the English.
lines.literal: miss, critical. board-the already come, but language English-its wrong type.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Salah ketik gimana?
lines.id: What sort of typo?
lines.literal: wrong type how?

lines.speaker: Yoga:
lines.text: “Wellcome”, pakai dua L. Tiga puluh papan, Mbak.
lines.id: “Wellcome”, with two Ls. On thirty signs.
lines.literal: wellcome, use two L. three ten board, miss.

lines.speaker: Bayu:
lines.text: Wah, siapa yang mau dijadikan kambing hitam, nih?
lines.id: Well, who's going to be the scapegoat, then?
lines.literal: wow, who which will be-made goat black, [nih]?

lines.speaker: Yoga:
lines.text: Jangan lihat aku, Mas. Filenya kan udah dicek Mbak Sarah.
lines.id: Don't look at me. Sarah checked the file, didn't she?
lines.literal: don't look me, brother. file-the [kan] already be-checked miss Sarah.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Yoga, jangan lempar batu sembunyi tangan. Revisi terakhir kamu yang kirim, kan?
lines.id: Yoga, don't pass the buck. You sent the final revision, didn't you?
lines.literal: Yoga, don't throw stone hide hand. revision last you who send, [kan]?

lines.speaker: Yoga:
lines.text: Iya, sih… Revisinya tiga kali, aku jadi bingung yang mana.
lines.id: Well, yes… There were three revisions, I lost track of which was which.
lines.literal: yes, [sih]… revision-the three time, I become confused which which.

lines.speaker: Bayu:
lines.text: Nah, itu masalahnya. Desainnya berubah terus, bagai air di daun talas.
lines.id: Well, there's your problem. The design kept changing, never settling on anything.
lines.literal: [nah], that problem-the. design-the change continue, like water on leaf taro.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Sudahlah. Sekarang bukan waktunya cari siapa yang salah. Saya juga salah karena tidak cek ulang.
lines.id: That's enough. This isn't the time to look for who's to blame. It's my fault too for not double-checking.
lines.literal: enough-[lah]. now not time-its search who which wrong. I also wrong because not check repeat.

lines.speaker: Bayu:
lines.text: Tenang. Pemilik percetakannya teman saya. Besok hurufnya bisa ditutup stiker. Nasi belum jadi bubur.
lines.id: Relax. The printer's owner is a friend of mine. Tomorrow the extra letter can be covered with a sticker. It's not too late.
lines.literal: calm. owner printing-house-the friend my. tomorrow letter-the can be-covered sticker. rice not-yet become porridge.

lines.speaker: Yoga:
lines.text: Mas Bayu penyelamat! Makasih banyak, Mas.
lines.id: You're a lifesaver, Bayu! Thanks so much.
lines.literal: brother Bayu saviour! thanks much, brother.

notes: **Gawat** — “critical, serious” — is what you say when something has gone badly wrong: *Gawat, Mbak!* In hospitals *gawat darurat* means “emergency”, which is where the abbreviation *UGD* (A&E) comes from.

**Kambing hitam** — “black goat” — is the scapegoat, the person blamed for everyone else's mistake. *Dijadikan kambing hitam* is “to be made the scapegoat”; the verb *mengambinghitamkan* exists and is standard, though it is a mouthful.

**Lempar batu sembunyi tangan** — “throw a stone and hide your hand” — means doing something wrong and then acting innocent or letting someone else take the blame. It is a sharp thing to say, and Sarah says it to Yoga as a boss, not as a friend.

**Bagai air di daun talas** — water on a taro leaf rolls about and never settles. KBBI glosses it as *tidak tetap pendirian*: someone, or something, that keeps changing. ⚠️ Learners often use it to mean “advice that doesn't sink in”; for that, Indonesians say *masuk telinga kanan, keluar telinga kiri*.

**Nasi belum jadi bubur** — Mas Bayu turns the proverb *nasi sudah menjadi bubur* (“the rice has become porridge”, it's too late) inside out: it's not too late yet. Twisting a well-known proverb like this is a favourite Indonesian joke, and understanding it is a sign you really know the original.

**Sudahlah** — “enough, let it go” — is *sudah* with the particle *-lah*, which adds a firm, final tone. *Makasih* is the everyday short form of *terima kasih*; *penyelamat* (saviour, lifesaver) comes from *selamat* (safe).

grammars.title: Talking about blame
body: Indonesian has a small, useful family of words for fault and responsibility. Notice that owning up (*mengaku salah*) is shorter and gentler than accusing (*menyalahkan*).

head: Indonesian
English
Example
rows: to wash one's hands of it

after: *Saya yang salah* — “I'm the one who's wrong” — uses the *yang* of focus you will study in Unit 17. It is the most disarming sentence in any Indonesian argument.
⚠️ *Salah* is also just “wrong” for facts: *salah ketik* (typo), *salah paham* (misunderstanding), *salah jalan* (wrong way). Nobody is being accused in those.

sections.title: Idioms from animals, food and daily life

blocks.text: Many everyday idioms are compound nouns: two ordinary words that together mean something new. You will meet these in chat, on TV and in the news within a week of listening for them.

head: Idiom
Literally
Meaning
rows: to become popular, be on the rise

blocks.text: *Jam karet* is how Indonesians themselves describe their relaxed attitude to time, usually with a sigh: *Maaf telat, biasa, jam karet.* *Dibawa ke meja hijau* means “taken to court” and appears in headlines constantly.

Proverbs still live in Indonesian public life: in speeches, sermons, newspaper columns and the *sambutan* at weddings. In conversation people usually quote only the first half and let the listener finish it — which only works if the listener knows it.

head: Situation
Proverb
Meaning
rows: a plan goes wrong, no going back
combining two aims in one trip
a loud person with little to say
Many a little makes a mickle.
The apple doesn't fall far from the tree.

blocks.title: Half a proverb is enough
items: *Ya, namanya juga nasi sudah jadi bubur…* — people often trail off after the first half, expecting you to nod.
*Berakit-rakit ke hulu…* is often all a parent says to a child who wants to skip studying. The rest (*bersakit-sakit dahulu, bersenang-senang kemudian* — suffer first, enjoy later) goes unsaid.
At B1 your goal is to recognise these, and to own two or three you can use naturally. Pick the ones you like the sound of.

blocks.text: Cover the Indonesian column, read the English, and rebuild each sentence from memory.

head: English
Indonesian
rows: Good morning. How can we help you?
*Selamat pagi, Bapak, Ibu. Ada yang bisa kami bantu?*
Right. If I want to speak, do I need to ask permission first?
*Baik. Kalau saya mau bicara, perlu minta izin dulu?*
A tourist-village festival? Very interesting. Who is coordinating it?
*Festival desa wisata? Menarik sekali. Siapa yang mengoordinasi?*
Excuse me, Mbah. I'm sorry to disturb you so late in the afternoon.
*Nuwun sewu, Mbah. Mohon maaf mengganggu sore-sore begini.*
Do I need to apologise to the family who were visiting the graves as well?
*Apakah saya perlu minta maaf juga kepada keluarga yang sedang berziarah?*
